content: The cases described in two reports were excluded from the analysis because they did not involve breastfeeding. One case involved a child who was never breastfed, while the other involved a child exposed to the Zika virus in utero and born with congenital Zika syndrome. These cases were not relevant to the outcome being studied. A cohort study involving women with confirmed Zika virus infection was identified, but only an abstract was available. This study reported on six women whose breast milk tested positive for Zika virus using RT-PCR. The evidence was downgraded due to risks of bias, imprecision, and publication bias. In one study, two mother-child pairs were reported, while three other studies each reported one mother-child pair. Another study described four mother-child pairs, but only one mother’s breast milk tested positive for Zika virus. In one case, exposure occurred at the 9th week of gestation, and the breast milk sample tested positive at the 36th week of gestation. The evidence was rated as very low certainty due to methodological limitations and other concerns. Parents of children with congenital Zika syndrome often report difficulties in feeding their children due to frequent choking and swallowing problems. This causes significant stress and anxiety, even when they have information on how to manage these issues. Parents fear making mistakes that could harm their child, such as causing suffocation. Feeding challenges also negatively impact bonding between mothers and their children. The burden of feeding, which is time-consuming and stressful, often falls disproportionately on mothers. Many parents feel that the information and support provided by healthcare professionals are inadequate, leading them to seek information on their own. Economic pressures, such as the need to purchase special foods, further exacerbate the challenges. In cases of severe disability or chronic encephalopathy unrelated to transmissible diseases, parents report not knowing how best to feed their child. Feeding difficulties are time-consuming and demanding, leading to frustration, stress, and concerns about bonding. Parents often feel that the focus on their infant’s weight gain by healthcare professionals adds to their stress. Training on feeding techniques, such as positioning to prevent choking and vomiting, can alleviate some of these concerns. In resource-limited settings, feeding problems are worsened by a lack of access to nutritious food, cooking facilities, and healthcare services. Mothers may lack financial support or assistance from fathers, further compounding the challenges. In some communities, failure to breastfeed is stigmatized and associated with contagion or infection. Alternatives to breastfeeding are often viewed as untrustworthy, and healthcare decision-makers emphasize the importance of building trust between providers and mothers to challenge established practices during disease outbreaks. Mothers report that advice from healthcare professionals with expertise in infectious diseases empowers them and gives them confidence in their feeding choices. However, they also experience stigma when unable to breastfeed, and their health can affect their ability to do so. Facilities that provide privacy for infant feeding can reduce stigma and improve the experience for mothers.
